subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
subtype: Approach: seeking advice from a trusted adult [Action]
passage: The community centre office smelled of tea and printer toner. Vasudha sat beside her mother's desk with her homework closed. “Amma, hypothetically, if someone at school was doing something unfair, and it was a friend, what would you do?” Vidya kept her eyes on her screen but stopped typing. “Unfair how?” “Just... breaking a rule that affects others. I can't say names.” “Then I won't ask.” Vidya told her about the year a co-worker padded the attendance sheets: she had first asked the colleague to fix it, then told the supervisor when nothing changed. “It cost me some warmth for a while. It didn't cost me my sleep.” Vasudha nodded slowly. “So talk to the person first. Then an adult if nothing changes.” “That's what I did. What will you do?” “I'll think about it tonight.”

qa.q: What did Vidya do first about the co-worker's attendance sheets?
qa.a: Vidya first asked the colleague to fix it, then told the supervisor when nothing changed.

qa.q: What might Vasudha be feeling about her friend's situation?
qa.a: Vasudha seems uneasy and unsure, since she cannot say names and wants advice without betraying her friend.

qa.q: What could Vasudha decide, now that she has this way of looking at it?
qa.a: Vasudha could talk to the friend privately first and speak to a teacher if the behaviour continues.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel about Vasudha's question?
qa.a: Vidya probably feels trusted and a little concerned, since she stops typing but does not push for names.

grounding: Unsure what to do, a student describes the situation to a parent without names, hears how the parent handled a similar choice and sees it more clearly.

subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
subtype: Approach: seeking advice from a trusted adult [Action]
passage:
Dear Papa,
Chandrika Didi said I should write to you since you're travelling till Sunday, so here goes. I'm not going to say who, not yet.
Someone in my class, a good friend, has been copying in tests. I've seen it twice. I don't know what to do. If I tell the teacher, I lose a friend. If I don't, it feels unfair to everyone who studies. Has anything like this ever happened to you?
Amandeep

Reply, 9:30 pm:
Aman, thank you for asking me. Yes. At my first job, a colleague I liked was fudging his hours. I stayed quiet for months and felt worse each week. When I finally spoke to him privately, he stopped. I wish I had done it sooner.
My suggestion: talk to your friend first, alone. If it continues, then the teacher. You don't have to decide tonight.
Papa

Next morning, on the fridge: Talking to her at lunch. Thanks, Papa. – Amandeep

qa.q: What was Papa's colleague doing at his first job?
How was Amandeep feeling when writing to Papa?
qa.a: Amandeep felt torn and unsure, worried about losing a friend and about unfairness to others.

qa.q: Why was describing it without names a good first step?
qa.a: It let Amandeep get Papa's advice and think clearly without getting the friend into trouble before deciding.

qa.q: How might Papa feel receiving this email while travelling?
qa.a: Papa was likely touched to be trusted, and glad to share his own mistake so Amandeep could avoid it.

grounding: Shows a student describing a friend's cheating to a parent without naming names, hearing how the parent handled a similar choice, and deciding more clearly.

subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
subtype: Approach: seeking advice from a trusted adult [Action]
passage:
Dhruv, you asked how I decided about the whole exam thing. I'm Gautam, and honestly, I didn't decide alone.
I was going round in circles for days. So one night, while Mum was folding clothes, I just said, “Can I ask you something hypothetical? No names.” I told her: a friend copies in tests, I've seen it, and I don't know if I'm supposed to be loyal or honest.
She didn't ask who. She told me about her own school: her best friend used to copy her homework, and Mum let it go for a year, then felt terrible when her friend failed the board exam, because nobody had pushed her to actually learn. She said, “Being loyal isn't always the same as being quiet.”
That changed how I saw it. It wasn't me against my friend. It was me for my friend, and for fairness.
So I'm talking to him tomorrow. And if that doesn't work, then Sir.

qa.q: What did Mum's best friend use to copy?
How did Gautam feel before asking Mum?
qa.a: Gautam felt stuck and confused, going round in circles about loyalty and honesty.

qa.q: What else could Gautam ask Mum before tomorrow?
qa.a: How to start the talk with his friend, so it sounds caring rather than accusing.

qa.q: How might Mum have felt sharing her own story?
qa.a: Mum may have felt a little sad remembering her friend, but glad the memory could help Gautam decide.

grounding: Shows a student describing a friend's cheating to a parent without names, hearing how she once handled a similar choice, and deciding more clearly.
